title: Terminal routes bypass workspace-scoped tokens
summary: Workspace ACL enforcement only extracts workspace ids from /api/workspaces/{id}/... paths, but terminal routes carry workspace_id in JSON body or query string under /api/terminal/..., so scoped worker tokens are not checked for terminal access.
trigger: Mint a token scoped to workspace A, then call POST /api/terminal/open with JSON body {"workspace_id":"workspace-B"}. The middleware sees no workspace id in the path and does not call AllowsWorkspace for B.
impact: A supposedly scoped worker can open/write/read/close a shell in another workspace if it has an agent-capable token. This reopens a multi-tenant isolation and host-exec risk after the workspace-scope hardening pass.

evidence.note: Terminal routes are /api/terminal/... and take workspace ids from the body/query, not a path segment.
Workspace-scope enforcement only checks workspaceIDFromPath.
workspaceIDFromPath only recognizes /api/workspaces/{id}/... paths.

failure_chain: A: Token scoping exists but the middleware only sees path-shaped workspace ids.
B: Terminal endpoints are shaped outside the workspace route tree.
C: Scoped tokens can drive terminal operations against an unscoped workspace id in the body/query.
D: The controller can no longer trust per-worker terminal isolation.
fix: Move terminal routes under /api/workspaces/{workspace_id}/terminal/... or add a pre-routing workspace extractor for body/query routes with a body-size cap. Require agent/admin role and add 200/403 tests for every terminal verb.
verification: Add a test that a token scoped to ws-a receives 403 for terminal open/write/read/close on ws-b and 200 on ws-a.
duplicate_check: New post-hardening finding. It refutes the blanket claim that per-worker workspace ACLs cover all workspace-bearing routes; related to but not a duplicate of XM-NEW-022.

title: Caller-supplied terminal_id can overwrite a live session and orphan the old shell
summary: Terminal sessions are keyed globally by terminalID and OpenTerminal uses Store rather than LoadOrStore/rejecting collisions. A second open with the same terminal_id replaces the map entry while the first shell and goroutines continue running.
trigger: Open a terminal in workspace A with terminal_id="x". Open another terminal in workspace B, or the same workspace, with terminal_id="x". The old session remains alive but is no longer reachable through terminalSessions.
impact: The first shell process/PTY/log pump can become unclosable through the API. In the cross-workspace case, this also interacts with the auth-scope gap and can hide a foreign process behind the new entry.

evidence.note: terminalSessions is a global sync.Map.
OpenTerminal accepts caller-supplied terminalID and stores by terminalID with no collision check.
CloseTerminal deletes only the currently mapped terminalID.

failure_chain: A: terminalID is caller-controllable after only syntax validation.
B: the session map key omits workspaceID and Store overwrites existing values.
C: the replaced session keeps its process/goroutines but loses the API handle.
D: sustained UI/agent use leaks shells and PTYs.
fix: Key terminal sessions by {workspace_id, terminal_id}; reject duplicate IDs per workspace with LoadOrStore; on collision never overwrite a live session; add a cleanup/reaper for old closed entries.
verification: Unit test two opens with the same explicit terminal_id; assert the second is rejected or the first is still closeable and no process is orphaned.
duplicate_check: Refines XM-NEW-013 after the direct cross-workspace requireTerminalSession check was fixed; the overwrite/leak path remains.

title: Terminal sessions still lack idle reaping and natural-exit map deletion
summary: The terminal close path cleans up explicit closes, but abandoned interactive shells can run forever, and naturally exited sessions mark closed without deleting the sync.Map entry.
trigger: Open a terminal and stop polling/closing it. Or let the shell exit by itself. No idle reaper deletes the session, and natural exit only flips a closed flag.
impact: Long-lived cockpit/agent sessions accumulate stale map entries and abandoned shells. This keeps the 50-100 MB budget typical rather than guaranteed.

evidence.note: OpenTerminal starts pump and Wait goroutines; Wait only calls markClosed.
pump closes the stream and markClosed records state but neither deletes the map entry.
Only explicit CloseTerminal deletes the map entry.

failure_chain: A: terminal lifecycle depends on explicit client close.
B: agents and browsers can disconnect without close.
C: processes/map entries survive until manual cleanup.
D: host RSS/fd budget drifts upward during sustained work.
fix: Add last-touch tracking and a terminal idle reaper; delete map entries on natural exit; make Close idempotent; expose terminal count diagnostics.
verification: Test natural process exit removes the map entry; test idle timeout terminates a fake shell and closes PTY/log descriptors.
duplicate_check: Known partial item in the status update, independently confirmed in code.

title: Concurrent plan approvals can start duplicate worker processes for one run
summary: ApproveRunPlan performs read -> status check -> save -> startManagedRun without a per-run transaction lock or active-process LoadOrStore. Two concurrent approvals can both see awaiting_approval and both launch workers.
trigger: Issue two concurrent POST approvals for the same awaiting run plan. Both handlers can pass the phase check before either save is visible to the other, then both call startManagedRun.
impact: Duplicate agent workers can mutate the same worktree/log/output. activeRunProcesses.Store by runID can overwrite one process handle, so CancelRun may kill only the last registered worker.

evidence.note: ApproveRunPlan reads, checks, saves queued status, then starts the managed run without a per-run lock.
startManagedRun always launches a goroutine.
runManagedProcess stores the process by runID, overwriting any prior handle.

failure_chain: A: JSON run state is read/modified without a run-level actor/lock in the approve path.
B: two approvals can both transition the same plan to queued.
C: both start a worker, and the process map retains only one handle.
D: cancellation, logs, verification evidence and cost accounting become unreliable.
fix: Wrap run transitions in a per-run lock or single-run actor. Use LoadOrStore for activeRunProcesses and refuse a second start. Make ApproveRunPlan idempotent after the first approval.
verification: Race test: 20 concurrent approvals of one run should produce exactly one start. Inject a fake command and assert active process count/start count is one.
duplicate_check: New post-hardening finding. Related to XM-NEW-007 retry duplication but hits the primary approve path.

title: Managed runs still have unbounded output buffering, no timeout, and no global concurrency bound
summary: runManagedProcess starts exec.Command without a context deadline, writes full stdout/stderr into a strings.Builder, materializes output.String(), writes the full output file, and calculates metrics from the full in-memory string.
trigger: Approve several long-running or chatty worker commands, for example yes-like output or a command that never exits. Each run gets a goroutine, process, log file, and full RAM buffer.
impact: A worker can OOM the Go API with output volume, or pin goroutines/processes indefinitely. The hard RSS budget cannot be guaranteed under adversarial or stuck agent load.

evidence.note: No global run semaphore or supervisor; every approved run gets a goroutine.
exec.Command is created without context and stdout/stderr go to an unbounded strings.Builder.
The full output string is materialized, persisted, summarized, and measured after wait.

failure_chain: A: each run is a detached process/goroutine with no global budget.
B: output accumulates in RAM until process exit.
C: stuck or noisy workers consume unbounded memory and fds.
D: host-safety claims fail under sustained agent load.
fix: Introduce a run supervisor with max concurrency per workspace/global, context timeout/kill policy, ring-buffer summary capture, streaming log file writes, and output-size caps.
verification: Fake command test emits >cap bytes and sleeps; assert memory capture is capped, log is bounded/streamed, process is killed on timeout, and run status is explicit timeout/cancelled.
duplicate_check: The status update names this as still open; this record verifies exact code paths.

title: Postgres mirror_seq ordering is process-local and can permanently skip updates after restart
summary: The mirror ordering fix uses an in-process atomic.Int64 and skips updates when stored mirror_seq >= incoming seq. After an API restart the counter resets to zero while old PG rows keep high mirror_seq values.
trigger: Persist a run to PG with mirror_seq=100, restart the API, mutate that same run. The new process sends seq=1; pgInlineUpsertRunSync sees storedSeq >= seq and commits a no-op skip.
impact: PG can remain stale after restart exactly when operators expect the mirror to survive process restarts. The queryable run index can lie until the new process sequence exceeds the old maximum and another mutation occurs.

evidence.note: pgMirrorSeq is a process-local atomic counter captured at dispatch time.
Existing PG mirror_seq is compared against the incoming process-local seq and skipped if greater/equal.
The incoming seq is stored in xm_runs as mirror_seq.

failure_chain: A: ordering number is process-local, not durable.
B: PG rows persist across restart with larger mirror_seq values.
C: new-process updates get smaller seq values and are skipped.
D: the mirror silently drifts from JSON after restart.
fix: Initialize pgMirrorSeq from SELECT max(mirror_seq) during schema/pool init, or replace it with a database sequence / wall-clock monotonic version / per-run durable revision stored in JSON and PG.
verification: Integration test: write seq N, reset the in-process counter or start a new process, save a newer run state, and assert PG reflects the new state.
duplicate_check: Refines XM-NEW-008 after the async ordering fix. The race ordering is fixed, but restart durability is not.

title: Core Go-to-Rust wrappers still lack timeout, output caps, and sanitized errors on hot paths
summary: RunSearch, RunChangetrack and RunSymbolgraph call coreCommand without context deadlines and buffer stdout/stderr fully into memory. Errors include raw args and stderr.
trigger: A hung or very chatty xmustard-core invocation from search/ground/impact wedges the HTTP handler and can allocate large buffers. A Rust/clap error can be reflected to API/MCP clients with internal paths/arguments.
impact: The per-call CLI substrate remains a DoS and information-leak point despite the binary resolver improvement.

evidence.note: coreCommand exists without context; coreCommandContext exists but is not consistently used.
runCore buffers stdout/stderr and returns raw stderr with no timeout.
RunChangetrack buffers stdout/stderr and returns raw stderr with no timeout.
RunSymbolgraph has the same pattern.

failure_chain: A: Go handlers spawn Rust per call.
B: key wrappers do not enforce deadlines or byte caps.
C: a hung child pins the request and a huge child output pins memory.
D: internal diagnostics leak into user-visible errors.
fix: Create one shared runCoreBounded(ctx, subcommand, args...) helper with timeout, max stdout/stderr, -- argument separation, sanitized client errors, and server-side logs; migrate all wrappers.
verification: Unit test fake xmustard-core that sleeps, emits >cap stdout/stderr, and exits with internal stderr; assert timeout, caps, and sanitized external error.
duplicate_check: Partly related to the v2 addendum bridge findings; still present after HEAD 422bbaf.

title: Binary-first bridge is incomplete; several runtime paths still require Cargo and source checkout
summary: Multiple rustcore helpers still exec cargo run --bin xmustard-core rather than the installed xmustard-core binary/resolver. A no-Docker deployment with only release binaries will fail these features.
trigger: Install xmustard-api and xmustard-core binaries without a Rust toolchain/source tree, then call repo-map/explain/semantic-impact/path-symbols or diagnostics/coverage paths using the same pattern.
impact: The documented no-Docker/single-binary deployment is only partly true. Operators hit feature-specific failures rather than one coherent bridge behavior.

evidence.note: BuildRepoMap hard-codes cargo run and buffers stderr.
BuildSemanticImpact hard-codes cargo run.
ExtractPathSymbols hard-codes cargo run.
ExplainPath hard-codes cargo run.

failure_chain: A: binary resolver was added to one bridge path.
B: other semantic helpers still assume Cargo/source.
C: packaged deployment becomes inconsistent by endpoint.
D: agent reliability depends on which tool path it happens to hit.
fix: Migrate all rustcore helpers to the same binary-first bounded helper. Keep cargo fallback only behind an explicit dev-mode env var.
verification: Packaging test with PATH containing only built binaries: call each rustcore helper or an HTTP endpoint that exercises it and assert no cargo invocation occurs.
duplicate_check: Refines XM-NEW-016. The status update says binary-first is fixed, but code shows only a partial fix.

title: Go LSP close still runs under the global session lock in acquire/release paths
summary: The idle reaper closes sessions off-lock, but acquireLSPSession and releaseLSPSession still call session.close while holding lspSessionsMu. close can spend up to the shutdown timeout and wait for the child.
trigger: Trigger a stale/root-mismatch LSP session and concurrently request definitions in another workspace/server. The first goroutine holds lspSessionsMu while closing/killing/waiting, blocking all session map work.
impact: A slow or wedged language server can turn cleanup into a global LSP stall. The reaper fix prevents orphaning but does not fully isolate lifecycle latency.

evidence.note: acquireLSPSession closes an existing session while lspSessionsMu is held.
releaseLSPSession closes the current session while lspSessionsMu is held.
close sends shutdown with timeout, kills/waits and closes stdin.

failure_chain: A: session map has one global mutex.
B: some close paths execute slow process cleanup under that mutex.
C: unrelated LSP lookups serialize behind process shutdown.
D: a bad LSP degrades all LSP-backed requests.
fix: Adopt the reaper pattern everywhere: remove session under lock, then close off-lock. Add concurrent close/acquire tests with a fake slow LSP.
verification: Test that acquire for another key is not blocked by a slow close on one key.
duplicate_check: New refinement of the LSP reaper verification request; direct child leak is fixed, lock granularity remains.

title: Go LSP frame reader has no header-line or Content-Length cap
summary: readLSPFrame reads headers with ReadString and allocates make([]byte, contentLength) with no maximum. A malicious or buggy LSP can send an unterminated header or huge Content-Length.
trigger: Run a fake LSP that writes a long newline-less header or Content-Length: 9223372036854775807. The Go side allocates or blocks without a protocol cap.
impact: The Rust LSP reader has a 64 MiB payload cap, but the Go LSP path can still OOM or hang the API process.

evidence.note: Headers are read via ReadString without a line/header cap.
Payload allocation uses Content-Length directly with no upper bound.

failure_chain: A: external language servers are trusted for framing.
B: a malformed frame controls allocation size or blocks header read.
C: one LSP process can OOM or wedge the API.
D: budget and availability guarantees are lost when LSP is enabled.
fix: Use a bounded reader: max header bytes/lines, max payload bytes, read deadlines via request context, and close the session on protocol violation.
verification: Fake LSP tests for oversized header, missing newline, and oversized payload; assert bounded error and session cleanup.
duplicate_check: Refines XM-NEW-020. The child reaper was fixed, but frame bounding is still open.

title: Recall still re-hashes every promoted memory before ranking and limit
summary: RecallContext loads all promoted entries and calls computeStaleness on every entry before ranking or applying the requested limit.
trigger: Create 10k promoted memories with path baselines, then call recall limit=1. The hot path performs O(history) file stat/hash work even though only one result is returned.
impact: The moat remains correct but can become too slow to use; operators may be tempted to disable drift checks, weakening xMustard’s key differentiator.

evidence.note: RecallContext loads promoted entries and computes staleness for all of them before candidate selection.
computeStaleness is called in an unconditional loop over promoted entries.

failure_chain: A: drift honesty is implemented synchronously at recall time.
B: every promoted entry pays path hashing before relevance ranking.
C: recall latency grows with memory history rather than limit/top-K.
D: governed memory becomes expensive exactly as it compounds.
fix: Rank on metadata/query/path/verification first, choose a bounded candidate window, drift-check only that window, cache file digests by content generation/stat, and optionally run a background invalidator.
verification: Benchmark and test: recall limit=1 over thousands of memories should hash at most K candidate paths and still flag stale candidates correctly.
duplicate_check: Known open XM-NEW-005; included because it remains the highest-value memory-moat fix.

title: MCP argument contract remains schema-thin and type-unsafe; remember still relies on query transport
summary: tools/list only declares minimal required fields, tools/call ignores unmarshal errors and coerces arbitrary JSON values with fmt.Sprintf, and the HTTP context route silently accepts malformed JSON bodies while falling back to URL query fields.
trigger: Call remember with content as an object/array or send a malformed JSON body to POST /context with content in the query. The server coerces or ignores shape instead of returning a schema error.
impact: Agents receive misleading tool contracts, durable memory content can land in URLs/logs, and bad calls become confusing runtime behavior rather than deterministic protocol errors.

evidence.note: remember builds content/title/source/paths into the URL query string.
tools/list schemas only include required fields and omit optional params/types/enums.
tools/call ignores json.Unmarshal errors and string-coerces all argument values.
POST /context ignores body decode errors and falls back to query params.

failure_chain: A: tool descriptions are the agent-facing API.
B: incomplete schemas and type coercion hide invalid calls.
C: remember transports sensitive durable memory in the URL.
D: memory quality, privacy, and agent self-correction suffer.
fix: Define per-tool JSON Schema including optional fields, additionalProperties=false, enums and numeric bounds; validate arguments before dispatch; send remember as JSON POST body; reject malformed bodies.
verification: Protocol tests: wrong types and unknown fields return JSON-RPC invalid params; remember content is sent in request body and never appears in URL path/query.
duplicate_check: Combines and verifies open XM-NEW-017 and XM-NEW-018 with an extra body-decode issue.

title: MCP bridge reads whole HTTP responses and echoes path-heavy API errors
summary: callAPI uses io.ReadAll on the entire API response body and includes method/path/body in returned errors. Large search/explain responses or error bodies can spike per-agent MCP RSS and leak details into the model-visible error.
trigger: Make the API return a very large response or error body; every xmustard-mcp process reads it all into memory and returns the raw error string.
impact: The one-MCP-process-per-agent model magnifies response-buffer spikes and noisy/internal errors across agents.

evidence.note: callAPI uses a 60s client but no response-size cap and returns raw API error text including path and body.

failure_chain: A: MCP process is per-agent and stateless.
B: bridge responses are fully buffered.
C: a large API result/error spikes the MCP process RSS.
D: internal paths/body text can enter agent context.
fix: Wrap resp.Body in http.MaxBytesReader/LimitReader, cap returned text, log full details server-side, and return structured sanitized MCP tool errors.
verification: Test API returns >cap body and path-heavy error; MCP result is capped and sanitized.
duplicate_check: New post-hardening bridge finding; adjacent to XM-NEW-024 but not the same root cause.

title: Auth middleware still reads/parses token stores twice per authenticated request
summary: authMiddleware resolves the bearer token and then calls HasAuthConfigured; ResolveToken and HasAuthConfigured each load env/file token records independently.
trigger: Under many agent requests with file-backed tokens, every request scans/parses the token file twice before routing.
impact: This is a medium DoS/performance issue and adds I/O to every API call. It also complicates future token rotation semantics.

evidence.note: Middleware calls ResolveToken and HasAuthConfigured on the same request.
HasAuthConfigured loads token records.
ResolveToken separately loads token records and linearly scans them.

failure_chain: A: token state is file-backed.
B: every request does two independent loads/scans.
C: concurrent agent traffic adds avoidable filesystem churn.
D: auth cost becomes visible on otherwise cheap endpoints.
fix: Introduce a small token-store snapshot cache keyed by file mtime/content hash with fail-closed corrupt handling, or combine enforcement and resolution into one load per request.
verification: Benchmark with 1/100/1000 tokens and assert one file read per request or cache hit; corrupt token file still fails closed.
duplicate_check: Known open item from the status update; verified at the exact call sites.

title: ListPrincipals drops workspace scopes for file-backed tokens
summary: ListPrincipals preserves workspace scopes for env tokens but returns only ID and Role for records loaded from the token file.
trigger: Mint a file-backed token scoped to one workspace, then list principals in the admin panel/API. The returned Principal omits Workspaces.
impact: Operators can misread a scoped worker token as global/unscoped or lose visibility into the intended ACL, which undermines auditability even if enforcement uses ResolveToken correctly.

evidence.note: ListPrincipals includes env principal scopes but reconstructs file-backed principals without r.Workspaces.

failure_chain: A: token scopes are part of the security model.
B: admin listing drops scopes for file records.
C: UI/operator view diverges from enforcement.
D: audits and token rotation decisions become error-prone.
fix: Return Principal{ID, Role, Workspaces: r.Workspaces} for file-backed records and add a token list test.
verification: Unit test MintTokenScoped then ListPrincipals; assert Workspaces is present.

title: Symbol graph build still caches whole file contents and recomputes query-time graph metrics per call
summary: The graph builder reads every indexed file into content_cache, while search recomputes hotspots and query-token document frequencies on every call after loading the cached graph.
trigger: On an 800-file workspace with large source files and frequent search calls, each Rust invocation rehydrates the graph, retains all file text transiently during rebuild, and recomputes O(symbols/edges) metrics per query.
impact: The cache is safer after atomic writes, but per-call CPU/RSS remains too high for the daemon target and 50-100 MB guarantee on large repos.

evidence.note: build_symbol_graph reads each file and inserts full content into content_cache.
hybrid_search recomputes hotspots per call.
hybrid_search recomputes document-frequency/idf structures per query.

failure_chain: A: warm cache avoids full parse but still deserializes and recomputes derived structures.
B: rebuilds keep file text around for edge extraction.
C: search cost tracks graph size, not just query size.
D: the daemon/mmap segment architecture remains the top P2 performance project.
fix: Move hotspots/idf/authority into persisted index metadata; stream edge extraction without storing every full file where possible; migrate to daemon-held mmap segments.
verification: Benchmark cold/warm search on a large fixture before/after; assert per-call allocations fall and coverage remains identical.
effort: 3-5 engineer-days as part of IndexEngine daemon
duplicate_check: Refines Cascade 2 after atomic-cache fix; not a correctness bug, but a budget/scalability finding.
